hook.text: On October 4, 2021, Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp vanished from the internet for six hours.

buildup.text: A routine BGP configuration change accidentally withdrew all routes to Facebook's servers.

discovery.text: Without BGP routes, DNS couldn't resolve facebook.com. The entire platform became unreachable worldwide.

twist.text: Engineers couldn't fix it remotely — their own tools ran on Facebook's network. They drove to data centers.

climax.text: One misconfigured command took down services used by 3.5 billion people. Cost: over $6 billion in revenue.

punchline.text: A single config change deleted Facebook from the internet.

quiz.question: What caused the 2021 Facebook outage?
options: A BGP configuration change that withdrew all routes

hook.text: In December 2021, half the internet broke. Netflix, Disney+, Slack, and Ring doorbells all went down.

buildup.text: AWS US-East-1, the oldest and most popular region, experienced a network disruption.

discovery.text: An automated scaling activity overwhelmed internal network devices, cascading into widespread failures.

twist.text: The AWS console itself was affected, so engineers couldn't monitor or fix the problem through normal tools.

climax.text: Thousands of companies learned a painful lesson: depending on a single cloud region is a single point of failure.

punchline.text: When one region fails, the world notices.

quiz.question: What caused the AWS US-East-1 outage in 2021?
options: Automated scaling overwhelmed internal network devices

hook.text: On June 21, 2022, major websites worldwide returned errors. Cloudflare, serving 20% of the web, was down.

buildup.text: A network configuration change was deployed to improve resilience in Cloudflare's busiest data centers.

discovery.text: A bug in the change caused 19 data centers to go offline simultaneously during a staggered rollout.

twist.text: The change was supposed to improve resilience. Instead, it caused the exact type of failure it aimed to prevent.

climax.text: Even infrastructure providers that protect others from failure are vulnerable to their own failures.

punchline.text: Changes meant to improve reliability can cause outages.

quiz.question: What irony marked the 2022 Cloudflare outage?
options: A resilience improvement caused the outage
They forgot to pay their bills

hook.text: On December 14, 2020, every Google service went dark: Gmail, YouTube, Google Docs — all of them.

buildup.text: Google's internal identity management system ran out of storage quota for authentication tokens.

discovery.text: Without tokens, no user could be authenticated. Every Google service that required login stopped working.

twist.text: The storage quota was set years ago and never updated as usage grew. A ticking time bomb nobody noticed.

climax.text: A forgotten configuration limit brought down the most reliable tech company in the world for 47 minutes.

punchline.text: Even Google can be taken down by a storage limit.

quiz.question: What caused Google's 2020 global outage?
options: The identity system ran out of storage quota for tokens
A power failure at a data center

hook.text: On June 8, 2021, Reddit, Amazon, the BBC, and The New York Times all went down at the same time.

buildup.text: Fastly, a major CDN provider, experienced a worldwide outage affecting 85% of its network.

discovery.text: A single customer configuration change triggered a dormant bug in Fastly's software, taking down the CDN.

twist.text: The bug had existed for weeks. It only activated when a specific, rare configuration combination was hit.

climax.text: The modern internet is fragile: a handful of CDN providers serve most of the world's web traffic.

punchline.text: One hidden bug took down half the web in seconds.

quiz.question: What triggered the Fastly outage?
options: A customer config change activated a dormant software bug

hook.text: On January 31, 2017, a GitLab engineer accidentally ran a delete command on the production database.

buildup.text: They were troubleshooting a replication issue and typed the command in the wrong terminal window.

discovery.text: 300 GB of production data was deleted. The team scrambled to restore from backups.

twist.text: Five different backup methods had all failed silently. The only working backup was a 6-hour-old snapshot.

climax.text: GitLab live-streamed the recovery on YouTube with full transparency. They lost 6 hours of user data.

punchline.text: Untested backups are not backups at all.

quiz.question: What made GitLab's database deletion so damaging?
options: Five backup methods had all failed silently
They didn't have any backup system

hook.text: In 2017, personal data of 147 million Americans was stolen from Equifax. Names, SSNs, birthdates — all of it.

buildup.text: A known vulnerability in Apache Struts had a patch available for two months before the breach.

discovery.text: Equifax never applied the patch. Attackers exploited the unpatched vulnerability to access internal systems.

twist.text: The attackers went undetected for 76 days because an SSL certificate for monitoring had expired.

climax.text: Two simple oversights — one unpatched server and one expired certificate — led to the largest data breach in history.

punchline.text: An unpatched server cost 147 million people their data.

quiz.question: What was the root cause of the Equifax breach?
options: An unpatched known vulnerability in Apache Struts

topics.title: Amazon S3 Outage and the Typo

hook.text: On February 28, 2017, a large chunk of the internet went offline because of a typo.

buildup.text: An AWS engineer was debugging S3's billing system and needed to remove a few servers from service.

discovery.text: A typo in the command removed far more servers than intended, taking down a core S3 subsystem.

twist.text: S3 hadn't been fully restarted in years. The restart took hours because the system was so large.

climax.text: Thousands of websites and services that depended on S3 went down. One mistyped command, billions affected.

punchline.text: A single typo brought down the internet's storage layer.

quiz.question: What caused the 2017 S3 outage?
options: A typo in a command removed too many servers

hook.text: In 2019, MySpace admitted it had lost all music uploaded between 2003 and 2015. Over 50 million songs — gone.

buildup.text: MySpace was migrating servers and the music files were stored without adequate redundancy.

discovery.text: During the migration, the files were corrupted or lost. No usable backups existed for the music library.

twist.text: MySpace initially claimed it was a glitch and would be fixed. Months later, they admitted the data was gone forever.

climax.text: Twelve years of independent music history — demos, first recordings, rare tracks — erased by poor storage design.

punchline.text: 50 million songs vanished from a failed migration.

quiz.question: Why did MySpace lose 12 years of music?
options: A server migration without adequate backups or redundancy

topics.title: The British Airways Data Center Fire

hook.text: In 2017, a power surge at a British Airways data center caused a cascading failure across all systems.

buildup.text: An engineer disconnected and reconnected a power supply, causing an uncontrolled power surge.

discovery.text: The surge fried servers in the primary data center. The backup data center failed to take over cleanly.

twist.text: BA had outsourced its IT operations years earlier. The institutional knowledge to recover quickly was gone.

climax.text: 75,000 passengers were stranded. The outage cost BA over £80 million in compensation and lost revenue.

punchline.text: A power surge grounded 75,000 passengers for three days.

quiz.question: What worsened the British Airways data center failure?
options: The backup data center failed to take over cleanly
They had no backup at all

hook.text: On February 28, 2018, GitHub was hit with 1.35 Tbps of traffic — the largest DDoS attack ever recorded at the time.

buildup.text: Attackers used memcached amplification: small requests to open memcached servers returned massive responses.

discovery.text: Each 15-byte request was amplified into a 750 KB response — a 51,000x amplification factor.

twist.text: GitHub was back online in 10 minutes. Their DDoS mitigation partner, Akamai, absorbed the traffic.

climax.text: The attack was massive, but preparation and a strong mitigation partner made recovery remarkably fast.

punchline.text: 1.35 Tbps of attack traffic, 10 minutes to recover.

quiz.question: What amplification factor did the GitHub DDoS attack use?

hook.text: On January 4, 2021, millions tried to log into Slack after New Year's. It couldn't handle the stampede.

buildup.text: Everyone returned to work on the same Monday morning, creating a massive simultaneous login spike.

discovery.text: Slack's infrastructure wasn't provisioned for the thundering herd of post-holiday reconnections.

twist.text: The problem wasn't total load — it was the spike pattern. Gradual load would have been fine.

climax.text: Thundering herd problems occur when many clients retry at the same time, amplifying the original spike.

punchline.text: Millions logging in at once can overwhelm any system.

quiz.question: What is a thundering herd problem?
options: Many clients retrying simultaneously amplify a spike
Too many servers processing at once
A database running out of storage

hook.text: In October 2021, Roblox went offline for 73 hours. Millions of kids couldn't play for three days.

buildup.text: A new monitoring system was deployed alongside a configuration change to their service mesh.

discovery.text: The combination created an unexpected interaction: the monitoring system overloaded the service mesh.

twist.text: Each fix attempt created new cascading failures. The intertwined dependencies made diagnosis incredibly hard.

climax.text: It took 73 hours because the root cause was an emergent interaction between two independent changes.

punchline.text: Two safe changes combined into a 73-hour outage.

quiz.question: What caused the Roblox 73-hour outage?
options: Two independent changes interacted in an unexpected way
A power failure at the data center

hook.text: In April 2022, Heroku discovered attackers had stolen OAuth tokens, compromising private GitHub repos.

buildup.text: Attackers accessed a Heroku database containing OAuth tokens for GitHub integrations.

discovery.text: The stolen tokens gave access to private repositories of Heroku users, including npm's private repos.

twist.text: Heroku revoked all OAuth tokens, breaking CI/CD for thousands of developers without warning.

climax.text: Storing OAuth tokens in a database without additional encryption turned a breach into a supply chain risk.

punchline.text: Stolen tokens turned one breach into thousands.

quiz.question: What made the Heroku breach widespread?
options: Stolen OAuth tokens gave access to thousands of GitHub repos

hook.text: On July 19, 2024, 8.5 million Windows computers crashed worldwide with the blue screen of death.

buildup.text: CrowdStrike pushed a faulty update to its Falcon sensor, a kernel-level security driver.

discovery.text: The update caused a null pointer exception in the kernel driver, crashing Windows immediately on boot.

twist.text: Because it crashed on boot, machines entered a reboot loop. Each required manual intervention to fix.

climax.text: Airlines, hospitals, and banks were paralyzed. It was the largest IT outage in history.

punchline.text: One bad update crashed 8.5 million computers at once.

quiz.question: Why was the CrowdStrike incident so hard to fix?
options: Machines crashed on boot, requiring manual intervention

hook.text: On August 1, 2012, Knight Capital lost $440 million in 45 minutes due to a software bug.

buildup.text: A new trading system was deployed, but old dead code from a previous feature was accidentally reactivated.

discovery.text: The dead code started buying stocks at market price and selling at lower prices — millions of times per minute.

twist.text: The kill switch didn't work. It took 45 minutes to identify which server was running the rogue trades.

climax.text: Knight Capital went bankrupt days later. Dead code that nobody removed destroyed a $1.4 billion company.

punchline.text: Dead code came alive and killed the company.

quiz.question: What caused Knight Capital's $440 million loss?
options: Old dead code was accidentally reactivated during deployment

hook.text: On May 6, 2010, the US stock market dropped 1,000 points in 5 minutes and recovered 10 minutes later.

buildup.text: A single trader placed a massive automated sell order using an algorithm, triggering panic.

discovery.text: High-frequency trading algorithms detected the sell pressure and amplified it by selling even faster.

twist.text: Some stocks briefly traded for $0.01. Others jumped to $100,000. Market prices became meaningless.

climax.text: Automated systems without circuit breakers created a feedback loop that nearly collapsed the market.

punchline.text: Algorithms panicking caused a trillion-dollar flash crash.

quiz.question: What amplified the 2010 Flash Crash?
options: High-frequency trading algorithms created a feedback loop
A power outage at the exchange

hook.text: In January 2021, Robinhood blocked users from buying GameStop stock during a historic rally.

buildup.text: GameStop's price surged 1,700% as retail investors coordinated purchases on Reddit's WallStreetBets.

discovery.text: Robinhood halted buying because it couldn't meet the collateral requirements at its clearinghouse.

twist.text: Users thought it was market manipulation. It was actually a liquidity and system design problem.

climax.text: Robinhood's system wasn't designed for the scenario where millions of users buy the same volatile stock.

punchline.text: Unprecedented demand exposed a design gap, not a conspiracy.

quiz.question: Why did Robinhood halt GameStop purchases?
options: It couldn't meet clearinghouse collateral requirements

hook.text: In 2018, TSB Bank migrated 5.2 million customers to a new platform. It went catastrophically wrong.

buildup.text: The migration moved decades of banking data from an old Lloyds system to a new Sabadell platform.

discovery.text: Customers saw other people's accounts. Some could access strangers' balances and transactions.

twist.text: The problems lasted weeks. 1.9 million customers were locked out. The CEO eventually resigned.

climax.text: Rushed testing, poor migration planning, and no rollback strategy turned a migration into a crisis.

punchline.text: A botched migration showed customers other people's money.

quiz.question: What went wrong with the TSB Bank migration?
options: Customers could see other people's accounts and balances
The new system was too slow

hook.text: On May 18, 2012, Facebook's IPO was the most anticipated stock launch in history. Nasdaq couldn't handle it.

buildup.text: A flood of orders overwhelmed Nasdaq's system. The opening was delayed 30 minutes.

discovery.text: A race condition in Nasdaq's matching engine caused orders to be lost or duplicated.

twist.text: Traders didn't know if their orders had been executed. Some accidentally bought twice the shares they wanted.

climax.text: Nasdaq paid $10 million in fines and $62 million to affected firms. A race condition in the busiest IPO ever.

punchline.text: A race condition ruined the biggest IPO in history.

quiz.question: What bug caused the Nasdaq Facebook IPO failure?
options: A race condition in the order matching engine

hook.text: On October 1, 2013, Healthcare.gov launched to serve millions of Americans. It crashed within hours.

buildup.text: The site was built by 55 contractors with no single technical owner. Integration testing was minimal.

discovery.text: On launch day, the site could handle only 1,100 concurrent users. Millions showed up.

twist.text: It took two months, a complete re-architecture, and a new tech team to get the site working.

climax.text: Healthcare.gov taught the US government that software projects need a single technical authority and real testing.

punchline.text: 55 contractors, no leader, no load testing — total failure.

quiz.question: What was a core problem with the Healthcare.gov launch?
options: 55 contractors with no single technical owner

hook.text: In 1999, NASA's $125 million Mars Climate Orbiter burned up in the Martian atmosphere.

buildup.text: The spacecraft approached Mars too closely and disintegrated due to a navigation error.

discovery.text: One team used metric units (newtons). Another used imperial units (pound-force). The values were never converted.

twist.text: The mismatch was flagged months before arrival. The warnings were dismissed as instrument noise.

climax.text: A $125 million mission was lost because two teams assumed the other was using the same unit system.

punchline.text: Metric vs imperial — a $125 million misunderstanding.

quiz.question: What caused the Mars Climate Orbiter failure?
options: One team used metric units while another used imperial

hook.text: On June 4, 1996, the Ariane 5 rocket exploded 37 seconds after launch, destroying $370 million in satellites.

buildup.text: Software from the Ariane 4 was reused in the Ariane 5. It had worked flawlessly for years.

discovery.text: A 64-bit floating point number was converted to a 16-bit integer. The Ariane 5's velocity exceeded the range.

twist.text: The code that crashed wasn't even needed during flight. It was a pre-launch calibration routine left running.

climax.text: An integer overflow in unnecessary code destroyed one of the most expensive rockets ever built.

punchline.text: An integer overflow blew up a $370 million rocket.

quiz.question: What caused the Ariane 5 explosion?
options: A 64-bit to 16-bit integer overflow in reused software

hook.text: Between 1985 and 1987, a radiation therapy machine gave patients 100x the intended dose. Six were injured, three died.

buildup.text: The Therac-25 removed hardware safety interlocks, relying solely on software for safety checks.

discovery.text: A race condition in the control software allowed the high-energy beam to fire without the safety filter.

twist.text: The bug only triggered when a fast typist edited the treatment plan in a specific sequence — hard to reproduce.

climax.text: Life-critical software must be verified with extraordinary rigor. Therac-25 proved the cost of failure.

punchline.text: A race condition in medical software cost lives.

quiz.question: What design flaw made Therac-25 dangerous?
options: It removed hardware safety interlocks, relying only on software
It used the wrong radiation type

hook.text: Toyotas accelerated on their own, causing crashes and deaths. Investigators found code with 10,000 global variables.

buildup.text: The engine control software was a tangled mess of spaghetti code that had grown over decades.

discovery.text: NASA's review found the code had no fail-safe for a stack overflow that could disable the throttle watchdog.

twist.text: Toyota blamed floor mats. It took external investigators to prove the software was fundamentally unsafe.

climax.text: Toyota paid $1.2 billion in fines. Uncontrolled technical debt in safety-critical code had lethal consequences.

punchline.text: 10,000 global variables in code that controls your throttle.

quiz.question: What did NASA find in Toyota's engine control software?
options: Spaghetti code with 10,000 global variables and no stack overflow protection

hook.text: An engineer pushes a bad config and takes down production. Traditional response: punish the engineer.

buildup.text: Blameless postmortems focus on what happened and why, not who messed up.

discovery.text: Google, Netflix, and Etsy pioneered this approach. It leads to more honest reporting and better fixes.

twist.text: Blaming individuals causes people to hide mistakes. Hiding mistakes prevents systemic improvements.

climax.text: The goal isn't to find who failed — it's to find what allowed the failure and fix the system.

punchline.text: Blame the system, not the person. Fix the process.

quiz.question: What is the goal of a blameless postmortem?
options: Finding systemic causes and fixing processes

hook.text: Every major failure has one thing in common: multiple safety layers failed at the same time.

buildup.text: Defense in depth means layering protections so no single failure can cause a catastrophe.

discovery.text: The Swiss Cheese Model shows that holes in each layer must align for an incident to occur.

twist.text: Adding more layers helps, but each layer must be independently maintained. Correlated failures bypass them all.

climax.text: Equifax had monitoring, but its certificate expired. GitLab had five backups, but none were tested.

punchline.text: Layer your defenses and verify each one independently.

quiz.question: What does the Swiss Cheese Model illustrate?
options: Failures happen when holes in multiple safety layers align

hook.text: A downstream service goes down. Your service keeps retrying, flooding it with requests, making things worse.

buildup.text: A circuit breaker detects failures and stops calling the broken service, letting it recover.

discovery.text: After a cooldown period, it sends test requests. If they succeed, traffic resumes normally.

twist.text: Without circuit breakers, cascading failures propagate across microservices like falling dominoes.

climax.text: Netflix's Hystrix library popularized this pattern. It's now standard in all resilient architectures.

punchline.text: Stop calling broken services — let them heal.

quiz.question: What does a circuit breaker do in software?
options: Stops calling a failing service to prevent cascading failures

hook.text: Netflix intentionally kills its own servers in production. On purpose. Every day.

buildup.text: Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances to ensure the system handles failures gracefully.

discovery.text: By breaking things on purpose, Netflix finds weaknesses before real outages expose them.

twist.text: Most teams are afraid to test failure in production. But untested resilience is just hope disguised as engineering.

climax.text: Chaos engineering isn't about causing damage — it's about building confidence in your system's resilience.

punchline.text: Break things on purpose to avoid breaking by surprise.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of Netflix's Chaos Monkey?
options: Randomly kill servers to test system resilience

hook.text: Despite decades of engineering, outages keep happening. AWS, Google, Facebook — nobody is immune.

buildup.text: Complex systems have emergent behaviors that no single person fully understands.

discovery.text: Normal Accident Theory says failures in tightly coupled, complex systems are inevitable, not exceptional.

twist.text: The goal isn't to prevent all failures — it's to detect them fast, limit their blast radius, and recover quickly.

climax.text: The best teams don't aim for zero failures. They aim for fast detection, small blast radius, and quick recovery.

punchline.text: Failures are inevitable — recovery speed is the real metric.

quiz.question: What does Normal Accident Theory say?
options: Failures in complex tightly coupled systems are inevitable
